issues: 'In 2019–20 alone, six of ten newly identified national laws were African' misstates the period and what was counted. Greenleaf and Cottier's February 2020 abstract counts the laws 'enacted or located' since the Global Tables of January 2019. That window runs from January 2019 to February 2020, not 2019–20 as a whole, and some of the laws were only newly located, not newly enacted. The wording is corrected.

Several claims in the correction had no source. The 2000s laws, ECOWAS 2010 and the enforcement-gap sentence are now sourced. The 2000s laws check out on Data Protection Africa's fact sheets: Tunisia Organic Act 2004-63, Burkina Faso Law 010-2004/AN, Mauritius Data Protection Act 2004, Senegal Law 2008-12 and Benin Law 2009-09. The ECOWAS Supplementary Act A/SA.1/01/10 was signed at Abuja on 16 February 2010, and its Article 2 obliges each Member State to set up a legal framework. For the enforcement gap, Data Protection Africa (updated February 2024) says many countries with laws face 'resource and capacity constraints to enforce violations'. The same page gives a scale figure that answers the myth directly: 36 of 55 African countries had a law as of January 2024.

Everything else checks out. Cabo Verde's Law 133/V/2001 (2001) was Africa's first comprehensive law, and the Malabo Convention entered into force on 8 June 2023. All three existing quotes are verbatim.

fieldFixes.correction: Cabo Verde legislated in 2001, and Tunisia, Burkina Faso, Mauritius, Senegal and Benin followed in the 2000s. West Africa's ECOWAS bound its members to harmonised laws in 2010, and the AU's Malabo Convention entered into force in 2023. Of the ten national laws that Greenleaf and Cottier newly counted between January 2019 and February 2020, six were African. By January 2024, 36 of Africa's 55 countries had a data-protection law. In most countries the gap is now enforcement: many regulators lack independence and the resources to act on violations.

issues: The last sentence overstates the scholarship. It says scholars treat 'them' (China's and Russia's laws) as 'a distinct state-driven model'. The only source is Anu Bradford's Digital Empires excerpt, which describes China's regulation of the digital economy as a whole as 'state-driven'. Russia is not mentioned anywhere in the excerpt (grep 'Russia' finds nothing), and Bradford's model covers digital regulation broadly, not data-protection law in particular. Reworded to attribute the model to Bradford, for China.

The data-localisation claim had no source on this record. It is correct for both countries. Russia: Federal Law 242-FZ of 21 July 2014, in force 1 September 2015 (kremlin.ru text, --check FOUND). China: PIPL Article 40 and Cybersecurity Law Article 37. The Russian source is added. 'Broad state access' is left as the author's general characterisation and is still unsourced.

The rest checks out. Federal Law No. 152-FZ 'О персональных данных' is dated 27.07.2006, and the kremlin.ru page also shows 'Принят Государственной Думой 8 июля 2006 года'. The PIPL was passed on 20 August 2021 and took effect on 1 November 2021 (PCPD). The access/copy/correct/erasure quote is verbatim. The PCPD quote does not state the 2021 date, so a date quote from the same page is added. The FALSE verdict fits.

fieldFixes.correction: Russia adopted its Federal Law 'On Personal Data' (No. 152-FZ) on 27 July 2006. China's Personal Information Protection Law was passed on 20 August 2021 and gives individuals the right to access, copy, correct and request erasure of their personal information. These laws bind companies strictly but sit alongside broad state access and data-localisation rules: Russia has required citizens' data to be stored on Russian databases since 2015, and China requires critical-infrastructure operators and large processors to store data domestically. Anu Bradford calls China's approach to digital regulation a distinct 'state-driven' model. It is a different kind of regulation, not an absence of law.

issues: The correction's opening clause is wrong. 'Work under the ITU–EU HIPSSA project began around 2010' is contradicted by the record's own ITU document: its foreword says HIPSSA ran 'from the very beginning of the project in December 2008'. The verdict should be FALSE, not MISLEADING. No part of 'dates from 2010' is supported: drafting is first attested in March 2011, validation was in March 2012, ministerial adoption in November 2012 and ITU publication in 2013. A 2010 date may come from confusion with the ECOWAS Supplementary Act of February 2010.

Independent check: the Future of Privacy Forum's 2024 report on African RECs cites 'The SADC Model Law (2012)'. The SADC model laws on e-transactions and cybercrime carry the same Gaborone 2012 validation and Mauritius November 2012 adoption text. The Windhoek 2011 validation found in search results belongs to a different SADC text (a universal-service toolkit), not the data-protection model law.
